utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning. Case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. For the Prosecution it's Daniel Saxon. My name is Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, and we are accompanied by case manager Ana Vrljic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you all. Standby counsel, good morning to you. MR. VAN DER SPOEL: Good morning, Your Honour. Tjarda van der Spoel, standby counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you. So I will start with the usual formality, explaining the purpose of reasons for Status Conferences such as this one. The last Status Conference was held on the 14th of June. The Trial Chamber is required, under Rule 65 bis, to hold a Status Conference every 120 days to organise exchanges between the parties, to ensure expeditious preparation for trial, and to allow the accused to raise issues in relation to his mental or physical condition. As I did on previous occasions, I'm just making it clear from the very outset of the Status Conference that this is a Status Conference, and both parties have a duty to adhere strictly to the purpose of the Status Conference. I do not have any intention to allow either of you to go beyond these limits as established in Rule 65 bis, and I will not hesitate to take whatever actions are necessary at any given moment if the proceedings are abused of or an attempt to derail them is there. I will start with the agenda proper, and of course the matter which is of the utmost importance at this stage and which is pertinent to every Status Conference is the ongoing process of disclosure. As I will explain very shortly, there are two main problems that have arisen and continue to arise, and the time has come to decide on these issues. As introduction, however, let me start by saying that in this ongoing process of disclosure, the Prosecution has filed four reports. The first one was filed on the 23rd of July of 2003. The second was filed on the 12th of February of 2004. So when we had the last Status Conference on the 14th of June, there were only two such reports available. Since then, another two reports have been filed. The third report concerning disclosure, which is partly confidential, was filed on the 13th of July, 2004. And very recently, a few days ago, on the last day of September, the 30th of September, the Prosecution filed its fourth report concerning disclosure. Because of the date, the proximity of the date of the filing of this fourth report, I want to make sure that the accused has received a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did receive the fourth report of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I thank you, Mr. Seselj. And following that, I just want to confirm the following, please, although I -- don't take it that I am doubting your words in -- as indicated in the fourth report, but I want to make sure that the following information is correct: I am informed that you filed or you attempted to file 81 witness statements in CD-ROM format, of which 23 are in Serbian language and that mention the accused's name. This you tried to do on the 5th of July, 2004, and the CD-ROM was rejected by the accused. It is your submission, I take it, that you consider your obligation under Rule 66(B) fulfilled. Then you attempted to file -- to deliver to the accused 70 statements in CD-ROM format of which 32 were in the Serbian language -- are in the Serbian language and mention the accused's name. You tried to hand these on the 20th of July, 2004. This is information, both this and the previous one, the disclosure of which arises under Rule 66(B). Again, once more you informed this Trial Chamber that the accused rejected the CD-ROM and that you consider your obligations under Rule 66(B) fulfilled. Then we have 19 witness statements in hard copy that mention the accused's name. Again, this was disclosed under Rule 66(B) on the 21st of July, 2004. These have been handed over to the Trial Chamber for -- to be redacted prior to being disclosed by -- to the accused. This matter is pending before the Trial Chamber, and we are going through them to see if they need to be redacted and to what extent. Then there is a potential -- what you describe as potential Rule 68, in other words, exculpatory or mitigatory material in hard copy in English and in Serbian related to the Croatian part of the case. This you disclosed on the 19th of August 2004. According to the information that you give me, this material was accepted by the accused. Then there is potential Rule 68 material in seven CD-ROMs relating to what you describe as "opposing forces." This you attempted to disclose on the 3rd of September, 2004. You informed me that the accused rejected these CD-ROMs and that you consider your obligation under Rule 68 fulfilled. Finally, also I suppose arising or in the wake of the decision of the Appeals Chamber to revoke our decision, previous decision or interlocutory decree relating to the Vojvodina element in the indictment, on the 3rd of September you disclosed a hard copy of analysis of Vojvodina population census in Serbian. This was on the 3rd of September. You informed me that the accused accepted the material. Now, going through all the documentation of the case and previous reports, I think there are two issues that have now come to a head and that need to be addressed thoroughly by you and the Trial Chamber and decided upon before we can even proceed any further. As you know, one of the basic reasons of the pre-trial stage is precisely the disclosure process that is imposed by our system, by our Rules, and it would be a big mistake for this Trial Chamber to ignore the fact that there are difficulties in this disclosure process, difficulties that have to be addressed. The first difficulty is the fact that the accused continues to refuse anything which is not in hard copy, that is, anything that is in electronic format. The problem arises, insofar -- in the light of the following two facts: First, that he rejects this material when it is handed to him in CD-ROM format or in any other electronic format while you consider your obligation under whichever Rule is applicable to have been fulfilled. This matter needs to be cleared up, because if it is fulfilled, then we have to move a step forward and decide how best to ensure that we can proceed forward preparing for the trial. If your obligations cannot be considered to be fulfilled, then we also have to find a remedy to ensure that they are fulfilled. So this is the first issue that has to be decided. The second issue relates only to basically Rule 68 disclosure in that while the accused pretends that even in the case of Rule 68, disclosures -- the material disclosed ought to be disclosed in his own language or a language that he understands. Although you have been forthcoming and cooperative, I must say, you still maintain that under the Rules you do not have an obligation to disclose Rule 68, to translate Rule 68 material into the accused's language if it is not in that language now. I think this is the second point that needs to be decided, because obviously on the outcome of such decision depends the other decision, whether you are fulfilling your obligations of disclosure under the Rules or not. It's important that these two points be decided at the earliest possible time. I have given this matter a lot of thought, and I think -- I think we cannot really pretend to proceed efficiently with the pre-trial stage until and unless these matters are decided. Since these issues are, of course, vital, I am not going to suggest that together with the other two Judges composing this Trial Chamber we will proceed to our decision without giving you an opportunity to be heard. The situation, as I see it, is as follows: The accused has made his position very clear. He has stated, "You cannot force me to accept anything which is not in the hard copy, and you shouldn't be disclosing to me Rule 68 material in a language which is not my own language." I am going to give the accused the option to go first if he wants to go first, not today orally because this is something that needs to be addressed in writing and thoroughly, but I will ask the accused whether he would like to file submissions in writing on this matter or whether he wants to rest it as it is and as I have explained it to the Prosecution, and then economise on time and allow you or give you the opportunity to explain to this Tribunal how, notwithstanding the fact that the accused is rejecting these disclosures, you would consider yourself to have fulfilled your obligations under the Rules. Mr. Seselj, would you like to be given the opportunity to file written submissions on these two matters that are interrelated and both -- both relate to disclosure or your rights to disclosure under the Rules, or do you prefer to leave it at that and pass on the bucket to the Prosecution to file written submissions arising out of your objections and your refusal to accept these documents? If you want time to think, I will give you time to think.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Agius, we have a different problem here. At the last Status Conference you asked me to submit to you in writing all my objections to these proceedings and to inform you about the problems that I face in relation to preparing my defence. I did that on ten handwritten pages, densely written, as part of submission 37. I have the impression that you have not read this at all. Hans Holthuis, the Registrar of the Tribunal, he deceived you in relation to the content of this. Allow me to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not going to allow you to finish because this Status Conference is not meant for speeches. This Status Conference is dealing with legal matters. I want to know from you a simple yes or no. This is a legal matter and has got nothing to do with the pages that you submitted earlier which contain no proper and thoroughly legal submissions. I'm asking you whether you want to avail yourself of the facility that I am offering you to submit submissions in writing, legal submissions, on whether there is anything at law which comforts your pretended right to refuse the matters or the material that the Prosecution is trying to disclose to you in electronic format and also in addition to whether the pretended right to have material translated or interpreted, translated into your own language arises also under Rule 68 or not. If you don't want to avail yourself of that opportunity, tell me no. If you want to avail yourself of that opportunity, tell me yes. But I only want an answer yes or no from you, no speeches. Otherwise, I'll cut you off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will never declare myself to you in terms of yes or no. Do not put questions like that to me because they have nothing to do with law or the science and practice of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I am going to decide this matter here and now. Following the explanation that the Pre-Trial Judge made earlier on, the accused is being given three weeks within which, if he so wishes, he may submit, within the parameters of the Rules and directives, written submissions covering the legal issues involved in the disclosure in electronic format and translations of documents of material disclosed under Rule 68. The Prosecution will have a further three weeks within which to respond and present their case, particularly explaining why, according to them, their obligations of disclosure under Rule -- under the applicable Rules, are being fulfilled. The Trial Chamber then will collegially decide these issues, these two issues. Next item is something that goes beyond. It's still related to disclosure but goes beyond what we have just discussed, and it's just the Trial Chamber and the Pre-Trial Judge giving information to the parties. There was, as you remember, a confidentially -- a confidential motion filed way back on the 23rd of April, 2004. This was Prosecution's Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond submission of additional information concerning protective measures for vulnerable witnesses. In response to the Trial Chamber's decision of the 11th February, 2004, which granted the Prosecution's request for the issuance of a non-disclosure order under Rule 53(A) of some witness statements that had to be disclosed under Rule 66(A)(ii) in which decision we ordered the Prosecution to provide more information to enable the Trial Chamber to determine the request for pre-trial protective measures, as I said, the Prosecution filed the confidential motion on the 23rd of April, and this submission provided general background information relating to the dangers involved in the present case, according to the Prosecution, due to the behaviour of the accused and provided more detailed information in relation to specific witnesses for whom protective measures were sought. At the last Status Conference, the accused stated that with respect to the protective measures sought by the Prosecution, his position was that the Office of the Prosecutor has no reason to assume that he could disclose documents that are explicitly described as not public or that he could disclose names of protected witnesses. The position, I suppose, is still the same. If -- we have not received any further documentation on this or any further submissions on this. The Trial Chamber, or I in particular, was, during the past months, involved in the drawing up of the decision in the final judgement in the Brdjanin case. As soon as that case was over, I have started working on this pending motion. I need to discuss it further with the other two Judges to see whether it's going to be a collegial decision or whether it's going to be only my decision. We are in the final stages of such discussions, and now that the Brdjanin case is over, I expect that we should be able to hand down this decision within a very short time. We are also doing our utmost to ensure that once it is handed down in the English language, it is translated immediately in the Serbian language and made available to the accused. The reason why I earlier on also raised the question or the urgency of the need to decide on whether disclosure is being carried out according to the Rules relates also to another motion that was filed in 27th July, 2004, it's a notice for non-disclosure of names and other identifying information. As I said the previous one, we are in a position to decide now because we are at an advanced stage. This one, I have gone into it, and I think at this stage we cannot proceed with even considering the merits of this motion, because as it is, during the last Status Conference the accused himself made a request to the Trial Chamber to order the Prosecution to disclose by the 14th of August copies of all Prosecution witnesses that mention the accused, and that prior to disclosing any witness statement in redacted form that this be submitted in toto to the Trial Chamber for approval. As I tried to explain to you, I mean until I had received the fourth report on disclosure by the Prosecution I had prepared to address this matter, in other words, the motion of the 27th July, thoroughly in the course of this Status Conference. However, since most of the documents that the Prosecution tried to disclose as promised, as undertaken, have been refused by the accused and now it needs to be decided whether this refusal is justified and whether the disclosure is legal or not, I think this matter has to be put forward, adjourned to when we are in a position to deal with it. So the discussion on this motion is being adjourned till after our decision on disclosure of electronic material and translations under Rule 68 -- Rule 68 disclosure is definitively decided upon either by this Trial Chamber or by the Appeals Chamber, as applicable. I come to Rule 65 material. 65 ter, I apologise. This matter I brought up during the previous Status Conference, and I think we need to take stock of where we stand now, because again this is another area where we need to register some progress. I also acknowledge that there are some difficulties, and some of the difficulties are also related to the points I mentioned earlier. You will recall that at the last Status Conference the Prosecution stated that it had prepared a draft of the pre-trial brief and that a draft -- also of a draft witness list and draft exhibits list. It also stated that it did not want to disclose these since they were not -- they had not yet reached the final stage. This was almost four months ago. Prosecution stated at the time that its assessment was that it had 63 viva voce witnesses and 40 92 bis witnesses, and currently - when I say "currently," it means at the time in June, mid-June of this year - around about 900 exhibits. The accused, according to my records, entered a declaration that his intention was to contest each of the 92 bis witnesses that you intended to bring forward. I take it that he was not only -- that his requirement is that these persons, these individuals be brought forward to give evidence here so that they can properly be cross-examined, cross-examined by him. According to the Prosecution, according to your declaration in June of this year, during the last Status Conference, you anticipated also that the number of exhibits would increase substantially depending if the accused -- depending on whether the accused agreed or did not agreed with the agreed facts which were proposed by the Prosecution. You will recall that we had started brushing the question of agreed facts during the last Status Conference, and I realised that the accused could be heading towards a difficult situation by even being asked to deal with these matters when he has a right to remain silent and also not to make any statements which could possibly incriminate him, and I stopped him. I'm glad that he stopped, and I am making it clear at this point in time that I will not allow any further discussions during this or any later Status Conference on possible agreed facts. This is a matter that I am going to leave entirely up to you and in which I am not going to be -- get involved any further. During the last Status Conference, Madam Prosecutor and the other members of the Prosecution team, you also informed me that you anticipated that you would be able to file 65 ter material, that basically what I mentioned earlier, the pre-trial brief, list of witnesses, list of -- and exhibits list, et cetera, by the end of the year, and I urged you to try and bring this date forward. Now, I honestly believe that what I mentioned before in relation to the problems that we have with regard to disclosure need not interfere with your preparations and fulfilment of the requirements under Rule 65 ter. I don't think the two issues ought to -- should be mixed, and one should not have a bearing on the other. So could I ask you, Madam Prosecutor, to update the Trial Chamber on, first, whether your anticipated list of 65 viva voce witnesses stands or whether you have revised this list. That's number one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the list basically stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Secondly, whether you are going to stick to your request to bring forward 92 bis witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What is your position with regard to the objection of the accused in relation to this, your request, and whether you object to their being brought forward for cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- brought forward for cross-examination, or are you going to leave this in the hands of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can make in relation to each and every witness a specified argument whether we concede that cross-examination should be allowed for this and that witness and for others not. So we would make -- in our submissions, we could make for each and every witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me make it -- let me make it very clear at this stage. When you come to this stage of fulfilling your obligations under the Rule 65 -- Rule 65 ter, you still need to indicate the -- all the details regarding these 40 92 bis witnesses that you propose to bring forward. The question as to whether you will be authorised to bring forward these witnesses under Rule -- Rule 92 bis will remain unprejudiced. We reserve the right to decide on that issue as we go along. As well, obviously, questions related to the accused's right to have these witnesses brought forward, in any case, for cross-examination, even if the examination-in-chief is substituted by Rule 92 bis statements. So all these matters will be left in abeyance pending eventual determination by the Trial Chamber, but you will need to indicate all the relative details in your list of witnesses. All right? Do I make it clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Saving, of course, any protective measures that will be put in place or will be in place between now and when you file the Rule 65 ter documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can already say that the pre-trial brief we will file this month, and the witness list we can file as soon as we have the protective measures decision. The exhibit list will take a little bit longer. We have not received anything in writing from Mr. Seselj in relation to agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I said please don't raise the matter again. I think last time -- I don't think this matter should be raised, at least not in my presence. Not in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, to be honest, at this point in time, since the accused is unassisted and he has decided to defend himself, it would be making a very big mistake if he responds to you on agreed facts. I made it clear to you last time, and I'm making it clear to you this time: Don't respond unless you decide not to agree with me. I think you would be making a big mistake if, without the proper legal advice, you try to respond to the matters submitted to you for acceptance as agreed facts. I will not deal with this matter any further, so please don't raise this matter any further. We may -- we may -- I might ask you for a final update at the Pre-Trial Conference when we come to that and if I am still in charge of the case, but until then, I am not going to have this matter discussed again during any of the pre-trial Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't intend to discuss this matter. The only thing I wanted to convey to you, that because there is no agreement on anything, the witness -- the exhibits list will take longer and we cannot make it in October. That is what I wanted to point out to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I prefer it that way rather than have the accused, without proper legal assistance, be asked to answer on what he agrees to and what he doesn't agree to and then find himself later on faced with his acceptance of certain facts as arguments used against him. And I will protect the accused because that's my duty and my responsibility. So -- so basically we've covered this. I would expect you, then, to proceed along your statement in relation to Rule 65 ter material. With regard to the pre-trial brief, this, I suppose, will be in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I would recommend to you that you start working on the translation into B/C/S as early as possible so that it can be handed to the accused without undue delay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- the Prosecution has a duty to file it in English and the Registrar has actually the undertaking to translate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean to say is please liaise with the Registrar to make sure there is no delay, even though I know that this is not your responsibility. And Registrar is here, present -- a representative of the Registrar is here present in the courtroom, and I'm sure that he will refer this to the Registrar. The Trial Chamber solicits the Registrar to give priority to translating the pre-trial brief into the language of the accused as early as possible. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to mention -- in relation to disclosure, I wanted to update you on two points. First of all, on the 30th of September, we tried to disclose another set of Rule 68 materials, four CD-ROMs, and it was rejected again on that same day. And secondly, if you are interested, it's always a question whether something needs to be translated into English, and we actually have prepared and could show it to you today an interview with the accused which shows that he clearly understands the English language. If you want to see it now, we could do it now. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What kind -- what kind -- is it a video recording or --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. It's a video recording of an interview. It's about two minutes and it actually shows that he can communicate in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, it's -- the ERN number of this -- this video is V0005068. So for reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you tendering it in evidence or not? You don't need to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. No. Actually, it's enough that it was viewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I'm not going to ask the accused to comment on that because the question is not whether he understands English or not at this point in time. That may become relevant later on, but the question is whether he is, under the Rules, entitled to have Rule 68 material disclosed in a language that he understands, in his own language or not. I think that is what is in issue for the time being, but of course the Trial Chamber acknowledges the -- what you are trying to prove by means of this video recording, namely that the accused does understand, according to himself, at least, does understand some English. Okay. I think I will not return to that matter again. There is another issue that we -- we need to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Agius.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to say something about this. I think you cannot deny me this right. I think that it is completely absurd what the Prosecution is doing. I am a slightly educated man. I have had some education so I have learned a little English, only enough to be able to communicate with these guards of yours. But because you heard me say three simple phrases in English, for you to conclude that I can study legal text in that language, a substantial legal text, that is something I cannot comprehend. And I do have the right to say something about it, however, you keep stopping me. You don't stop the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because, Mr. Seselj, you don't need to explain all this to me or to the Trial Chamber. What -- what we have seen here and what you have stated, I don't think at the present moment any of this is important, because as I said, it's a question of whether you have a right to have Rule 68 material disclosed in your language or whether the Prosecution can pretend to fulfil their obligations under Rule 68 to disclose them only in the English language or whichever language they may have it. So that's the question of whether you know English. How much English you know is completely irrelevant for the purpose of the exercise that I particularly have to embark upon. So don't worry about how much English you know. You have your rights under the Statute and under the Rules, and they will be respected. If the decision of the Trial Chamber is that they need to be translated in your own language, they will be translated in your own language. Earlier on, in one of the previous Status Conferences, we discussed the accused's submission. He numbers his submissions, and this is very convenient for the purpose of the Pre-Trial Chamber. I'm referring to submission number 37, filed way back in July of 2004. The question is -- or refers to an earlier matter that the accused had raised, namely he was asking the Registrar to furnish him with all the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. By "jurisprudence," he was also meaning not only decisions but also parties' submissions in his own language and presumably in hard copy. And the Registrar or the Deputy Registrar at the time had answered his request on 11 June, that is a couple of days before the last Status Conference, stating that in order to be able to comply with the accused's request, the Registrar -- the Registry would have to provide with thousands of documents amounting to tens of thousands of pages and that this was neither practical nor reasonable. The Registrar was, however, amenable and also able to accommodate a more limited and focused request. You recall that I had allowed a brief discussion on this issue, particularly explaining two matters: One, that this is basically a matter to be resolved between the accused and the Registrar and that the Trial Chamber would involve itself in this issue only insofar as the rights of the accused to be able to defend himself could be at stake. You will recall also that we went -- I gave the accused the opportunity to explain in a little bit more detail his grievance particularly in relation to the disclosure of case law, of decisions of this Tribunal, and you will recall that he had particular complaints with regard to some decisions of this Tribunal that had not been given to him presumably at the time, and I think that was the position because they had not yet been translated into B/C/S or they were still being in the process of being translated into B/C/S. I have, in preparation for this Status Conference, tried to check what the situation is. I haven't really checked on what has been disclosed because I think I can ask the Registrar to update the Trial Chamber formally, formally during the Status Conference. There was one problem that I discovered, actually, and that is that the Kupreskic judgement, which was delivered quite some time ago, had not yet been translated. I made further inquiries to see if some progress could be reported on this matter. I learnt this morning that there are good news also on Kupreskic, and I now call on the Deputy Registrar present in this courtroom to update the Trial Chamber on what has been furnished to the accused in accordance with the -- or along the lines indicated in the previous Status Conference. If you could update the Trial Chamber, please, the Pre-Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can inform you that we delivered the following translations, Serbian translations of the following judgements: The judgements in the Jokic case, the judgements in the Deronjic case, and the judgement in the Simic case, the judgement in the Mrdja case, the judgement in the -- the appeals judgement in the Krnojelac case, the judgement in the Babic case, the judgement in the Nikolic case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which Nikolic? Momir? Dragan?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic. The judgement in the Mucic case, the judgement in the Obrenovic case, and the judgement in the Cesic case. I can tell you as well that I have here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you proceed any further. Did you -- are you in a position to confirm that the Appeals Chamber decision reversing our -- the interlocutory decree on the Vojvodina element and the -- has been -- whether it has been disclosed or given to the accused in his own language?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I can confirm that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And what else were you going to state?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have here in my hands a list with all the 48 translations -- in B/C/S translations of judgements we have at this point in time, and if -- we can deliver this list to the accused, and if he needs some of these judgements, if he still does not have one of these judgements, he can simply ask us and we will deliver him these judgements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher. Is it in English?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's in B/C/S. So, Usher, could you please hand that to the accused. At this point, Mr. Seselj, if there are still any other judgements that you require -- I know that you require them all. If there are any judgements that have not been handed down to you in your language, could you please bring that to my attention, and I will work on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Agius, the representative of the Registry has not said - or at least I did not hear it - what his answer is to your direct question as to the Kupreskic judgement. Does this judgement exist in the Serbian language? He hasn't mentioned it. They're avoiding giving me this judgement for special reasons. Because this judgement was made several years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Registrar, please. What is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do have some information myself, because I checked, but I don't know if you have come prepared to furnish -- to provide the Trial Chamber with this information. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Translation Unit informed me -- informed me that they can deliver the translation within this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Within this week. Okay. So the position is -- this is the information that I was given, too, but I mean, I had no possibility of confirming it with the translation unit. But I am informed, and the Registrar confirms it, that within this week you should be given -- handed a copy of the Kupreskic judgement. So I haven't gone through that list. I haven't seen it, actually, I don't know if there are any other judgements that are missing, that have not yet been handed to you. If there are, please bring them to my attention, and I will make sure that they are handed to you at the earliest possible, as I promised last time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Agius, there are many judgements missing. The Krstic appeals case, the Blaskic appeals case, and so on and so forth. However, I wish to draw your attention to another problem. Every time before a Status Conference, two or three days before, I receive several judgements from the Registry, and then I get nothing until the next Status Conference. Then they give me a few more to show that they have fulfilled at least a part of their obligations. Their obligation is to disclose to me or send to me all the judgements as soon as possible, because I have to become familiar with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, especially in view of the fact that this is a specific jurisprudence which I have not been able to familiarise myself with anywhere else. I will have to submit a pre-trial brief. I have to familiarise myself with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal to see what it looks like in practice. I know what it's like in theory on the basis of the Rules, but I have to see what it looks like in practice. And it is your duty to make it possible for me to familiarise myself thoroughly with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. If a hundred thousand pages are a problem for you, they're not a problem for me. I can study a hundred thousand pages. I have studied thousands of pages all my life. You say it's not rational. It is rational for me to have everything at my disposal. When the Prosecution delivers to me their motions, in my submission number 37 I quoted many of them but I don't have any of these decisions, any of these judgements. How then can I challenge the position of the Prosecution unless I get all this material in Serbian where I can find arguments to oppose what the Prosecution is saying? They rely on God knows what, and all I can do is take their word for it because there is nothing else I can rely on. That is why I have to familiarise myself with the entire jurisprudence of this Tribunal exclusively in the Serbian language because this is the only language I understand, and it all has to be in writing in hard copy. As for searching the database of the Prosecution, I submitted a request to the Registry to allow me to hire somebody I trust to search this for me, someone who is skilled at working on a computer, and then this person could search the Prosecution database that they make available. But although this summer you changed Article 68 of the Rules, subparagraph (1) is also something that is favourable to me because the first paragraph is not brought into question. Everything has to be delivered to me in hard copy and in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I realise that a hundred thousand pages will not be a problem for you, Mr. Seselj. In fact, you've spent the last five minutes saying a lot of words without giving me the answer I requested from you. I just said if there are any other decisions in that list that you have not yet received, and you mentioned one or two only, then please let me know. So go through that list. Not now, later on. If there are any other decisions included in that list which should be made available to you in your language and they haven't yet been made available to you, bring that to my attention. I'll try to find out why this is so and make sure that they are handed to you as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Agius.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the matter ends there. Go through it, and when you have further information for me, then make me aware of it, give me the details, and I will do the rest. But there is no point in discussing it any further. You can rest assured that if you require all Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the decisions of this Tribunal in your language, you will get them all. It's not a question of hard copy because they exist in hard copy, and it's not a question of volume. That's not my problem. And there should be no problems. There are maybe a few other things left. I just wanted to make sure that everyone is aware that the appeals decision on the interlocutory -- Appeals Chamber's decision on the interlocutory appeal concerning jurisdiction was decided on the 30th of August, and this reverts us back to the position as it was previous to our decision. In other words, as far as the indictment is concerned. The question on the rights of the accused to -- the question on the accused's motion for provisional release was decided. I am not aware of any appeal on that. If there has been one, I would be glad to know. And that brings us to the last part of the Status Conference. As I said in the beginning, I am bound to inquire on the state of the accused. I'm referring only to your state of health and the condition of detention. We'll start with your state of health. Is there any matter related to your health that you would like to bring to my notice, Mr. Seselj? And then we'll talk about the condition of detention afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you going to make it possible for me to raise some status related questions? I have two status related questions that are very important and that are more important than the condition of my health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one, yes. Start with the first status question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Agius, you talked about my submission 37 a few minutes ago. By your decision dated the 6th of July, you gave instructions that my submission 37 should not be disclosed to the public, with the argumentation that is not contained at all in my submission 37. You forbade it to be made public on the basis of something that does not exist in submission 37. That is what I've been trying to tell you from the very beginning of this Status Conference. You have been given something completely different and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have cut you off. And if you're trying -- if I did that and you're trying to make public what I said will not be public, you will not be given a chance. So if you want to make further submissions on this, file them in writing, Mr. Seselj. Next point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no intention of disclosing something that you forbade to be disclosed. But I would like to draw your attention to something; namely, you forbade the publication of something that simply does not exist in my text. Please read my submission 37 and you will see that that, on the basis of which you forbade it, simply does not exist in my text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to the second point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 19th of August, I received some material from the Prosecution on the basis of Rule 68. This is material that is open to the public, and it was handed in earlier on to Slobodan Milosevic, as it says here, and the Prosecution believes that these -- this material can be of an apologetic nature. It's supposed to be exculpatory, but this is the word they used. It contains only quotations from certain documents. Since these documents are very important for my defence, and the statement of Zivota Panic is particularly relevant - he confirmed here that all the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were within the JNA and that they were very disciplined - I insist that all these documents be handed over to me in their entirety, not only certain quotations, because perhaps these are not the most important quotations, perhaps these are not the most important pants. Secondly, I insist that the Prosecution supplies me with all the material they have about the war activities of the Serbian Guard that was established by Vuk Draskovic and the Serbian Renewal Movement. It consisted of Belgrade criminals. Because this material will be very important for my defence. I have learned for a fact that they have a lot of such material from Gospic, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, et cetera, et cetera. So in order to prevent any kind of confusion and any kind of confusion regarding the role of different factors in this war, I ask you to instruct the Prosecution to provide me with all this material. So anyway, if they provide me with any material, they should do so in the entirety of those materials. So if they left out a particular sentence and so on and so forth, then I can say, "Well, you've left out a particular sentence, and so on," but I believe it is impermissible in serious court proceedings to give only sections of documents or quotations rather than the entire documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if Mr. Seselj knows this or not, but basically we don't see -- none of the three Judges receive copies of what is disclosed to you. We don't get copies of those, of that material. So basically I have a note here that potential Rule 68 material in hard copy in English and Serbian related to the Croatian part of the case was disclosed to you on the 19th of August and that you accepted that material, but I don't know what it is. So what I suggest is the following: I will now address the Prosecution and see if you are in a position to respond to Mr. Seselj's request here and now. If not, I will invite Mr. Seselj to file a proper motion addressing particularly this material about which I know absolutely nothing, because we don't receive this material, and then you will have an opportunity to respond. I don't know which one you prefer. But are you in a position to deal with Mr. Seselj's submissions or requests?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can actually do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the documents where Mr. Seselj mentioned that he received only quotations from larger documents, that is correct. It's actually quotations from witness statements of sensitive sources where we have already indicated in our general submission how we would do disclosure. We have already mentioned that we would not disclose the entire statement of these sensitive sources in other cases but just bring the quote that relates to Seselj. And the same material was provided to Mr. Milosevic, and he also didn't get anything else than quotes from these statements. In relation to the Serbian Guard, Vuk Draskovic, we disclosed what is Rule 68 or potential Rule 68. The fact that other groups unrelated to Mr. Seselj commit crimes throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, I can't see how that can, in any event, be exculpatory for this accused. Therefore, we do not intend to provide this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I think this calls for a proper motion on your part, because I don't know what, in actual fact, for all intents and purposes, it's as if you're talking at cross-purposes, because since we do not receive the material that is handed to you, we are not in a position to -- we are not in a position to really know what needs to be decided. I think first issue that needs to be decided relates to this material that was disclosed on the 19th of August, whether the abridged or redacted or whatever information disclosed suffices according to the Rule or whether it's the case of disclosing more or the entirety. That's the first thing that needs to be decided. And secondly, your request as it relates to -- I don't know which movement you mentioned. One needs to see whether that falls under Rule 68 or not, and if it doesn't fall under Rule 68, whether it's something that can be researched in the Prosecution database if you're given this assistance, researched under Rule 68(i), or whether it has to be disclosed under some other kind of -- under some other Rule. So please file an ad hoc motion so that I can then communicate to the Prosecution and decide these issues, because they are not necessarily Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond related, the one to the other. The first one relates to what has already been disclosed; the other relates to material that has not been disclosed and which you pretend to have disclosed, which the Prosecution is telling you this is not -- has got nothing to do with you or with the case. So we need a proper motion. Your state of health. Are there any particular complaints that -- or matters you would like to raise in regard to your health?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Agius. Today several times you stated that I was pretending, and then you stated that I speak for a long time and I do not say anything, especially not in respect of what you had asked me about, and this caused additional suffering in my part and in addition to all the suffering that your robes cause me. If you're going to prevent me from speaking again, I have decided to look at you all the time regardless of how great and deep my suffering may be. However, I must say that what you stated today is not really something that a Judge in any court in this world should say. I defend myself as I deem most expedient for these proceedings. I know that this is going to cause additional hatred on your part and on the part of the Prosecution, but that is your own affair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. With regard to your condition of detention in the unit, do you have any complaints?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that basically brings an end to today's Status Conference. The next one will be convened in accordance with the Rules, that is within 120 days from today. The Pre-Trial Chamber stands adjourned, and the Status Conference stands adjourned.
